name: Steal Application Access Token
summary: Adversaries can steal application access tokens as a means of acquiring credentials to access remote systems and resources.

name: Active Scanning: Scanning IP Blocks
summary: Adversaries may scan victim IP blocks to gather information that can be used during targeting. Public IP addresses may be allocated to organizations by block, or a range of sequential addresses.

name: Active Scanning: Vulnerability Scanning
summary: Adversaries may scan victims for vulnerabilities that can be used during targeting. Vulnerability scans typically check if the configuration of a target host/application (ex: software and version) potentially aligns with the target of a specific exploit the adversary may seek to use.

name: Active Scanning:  Wordlist Scanning
summary: Adversaries may iteratively probe infrastructure using brute-forcing and crawling techniques. Wordlists used in these scans may contain generic, commonly used names and file extensions or terms specific to a particular software.

name: Active Scanning
summary: Adversaries scan victim-facing services and networks to discover exposed hosts, ports, and vulnerabilities. Findings feed later targeting and initial-access decisions.

name: Acquire Infrastructure
summary: Adversaries purchase or register servers, domains, and other infrastructure for use in campaigns. This infrastructure commonly supports phishing, command and control, and staging later in the attack lifecycle.

name: Phishing: Spearphishing Attachment
summary: An adversary sends a targeted email carrying a malicious attachment to gain initial access.

name: Command and Scripting Interpreter: PowerShell
summary: Adversaries use PowerShell to execute commands and scripts on Windows hosts. Its native availability and access to the .NET framework make it a common execution and download tool.

name: User Execution: Malicious File
summary: Adversaries rely on a user executing a malicious file delivered by another means, such as an email attachment or a web download. Execution typically follows initial access and precedes follow-on tooling.

name: Scheduled Task/Job: Scheduled Task
summary: Adversaries abuse the Windows Task Scheduler to run programs at system startup or on a schedule. Tasks provide persistence and can launch malicious binaries under a trusted system process.

name: Create Account
summary: Adversaries create local or domain accounts to maintain access to systems. New accounts can blend in with legitimate administration when monitoring is weak.

name: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder
summary: Adversaries add Run keys and Startup-folder entries so programs execute at boot or logon. The technique provides persistence and, in some configurations, elevation.

name: Valid Accounts
summary: Adversaries use compromised but legitimate credentials to access systems and blend with normal activity. Valid accounts defeat many perimeter controls and complicate attribution.

name: Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Tools
summary: Adversaries disable or tamper with security software, logging, and monitoring tools. The goal is to remove visibility before continuing the intrusion.

name: OS Credential Dumping: LSASS Memory
summary: Adversaries dump the LSASS process memory to extract credentials. Output commonly yields plaintext passwords, hashes, and tickets for lateral movement.

name: Account Discovery
summary: Adversaries enumerate local and domain accounts to map identities and privileges. Results guide targeting of valid accounts and groups.

name: Remote Services: Remote Desktop Protocol
summary: Adversaries move laterally using Remote Desktop Protocol between Windows hosts. Interactive sessions enable direct access to systems, tools, and data.

name: Email Collection
summary: Adversaries gather email from local stores, servers, or cloud mailboxes. Collected mail supports both intelligence gathering and further phishing.

name: Ingress Tool Transfer
summary: Adversaries transfer tools and payloads into the compromised environment. Common channels include command-and-control protocols and legitimate cloud services.

name: Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols
summary: Adversaries communicate over HTTP and HTTPS to blend command-and-control traffic with normal web activity. Web protocols are commonly allowed outbound and hard to distinguish without inspection.

name: Exfiltration Over C2 Channel
summary: Adversaries exfiltrate data over the same channel they use for command and control. Reusing the channel avoids extra connections and blends with existing traffic.

name: Data Encrypted for Impact
summary: Adversaries encrypt victim data to disrupt availability and extort payment. Ransomware operations commonly pair this with data theft.
